crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how a clinical or operational setting prepares for, deploys, and monitors artificial intelligence systems.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are AI systems that run inference and often training or fine-tuning within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, rather than sending protected health information to external cloud services.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage refers to systematic differences in how an AI system assigns urgency, acuity, or priority to patients based on characteristics such as race, sex, age, language, insurance status, or disability.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware, from infusion pumps and patient monitors to imaging systems and implantable devices, against unauthorized access, data interception, and manipulation.

sections.body: Governance, compliance and medical device security is the part of AI in medicine that deals with rules, oversight and safety, and AI is not only the subject of regulation but also a tool for regulation. Enablement audits use AI to check whether clinical AI tools are deployed correctly and fairly, while local models run on hospital hardware so patient data stays inside the institution. Software as a medical device is a regulatory category for AI that diagnoses or treats, and bias in clinical triage is a known failure mode that AI is used to detect and measure. Security of connected medical devices involves monitoring for intrusions and anomalies.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this work are solved. Local models for patient data are technically feasible and are used in practice. Software as a medical device has clear regulatory pathways in several countries. But bias in clinical triage is not solved, because bias can enter through training data, feature selection or deployment context. Security of connected medical devices is not solved either, because new vulnerabilities appear as devices are updated and networked. The site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that the legal and human stakes are not hypothetical.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare sets out how hospitals verify that AI tools are working as intended. Local Models for Patient Data then explains the technical choice to keep data on premises, which is a common compliance strategy. Software as a Medical Device covers the regulatory classification that determines what evidence a developer must produce. Bias in Clinical Triage examines a specific failure mode that audits are meant to catch. Security of Connected Medical Devices addresses the network risks that arise when devices share data. Together these pages move from process to architecture to regulation to fairness to infrastructure.
